summary:
Aydın province stands under the national framework that applies across Turkey, and that framework has been revised to place documented LGBT people under sustained legal jeopardy. The Turkish Ministry of Health announced new reporting rules in September 2025 that require hospitals to record the gender of transgender patients in official e-reports rather than allowing them to enter an "other" option, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular listing "gender reassignment" as an official cause for medical-board referral. The stated purpose was to tighten transition-related care; the practical effect is that every clinical encounter leaves a documented marker of a trans patient's status.

Human Rights Watch described the measure as an attempt to silence doctors, and that concern sits alongside a wider tightening reported by Kaos GL in its 2025 monitoring, which found anti-LGBTI+ hostility institutionalised as explicit state policy, with senior officials issuing hate speech and instructions to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner. Regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom during the same period.

The Erdoğan government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Under that framing a draft legislative package that would effectively criminalise LGBT people was before the government as of October 2025. The measure had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Street-level enforcement in Istanbul illustrates that point. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The passport-carrying rule for foreigners compounds these risks. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor in Aydın's coastal towns, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Turkish rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex — a trans man had been held in a women's prison — and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited here as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.
tangentialFactors:
The draft package reported on 29 October 2025 would amend both the Turkish penal code and the civil code, criminalising behaviour deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" and making participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony punishable by up to four years in prison. It would also raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25 and impose mandatory permanent infertility, while penalising the health professionals who provide such care. Human Rights Watch characterised the draft as one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades, and fifteen Turkish LGBT groups together with the Turkish Medical Association were recorded as opposing it.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at its launch, concluded that hostility toward LGBTI+ people had moved from social prejudice to administrable policy: instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner, hate speech by senior officials, and systematic curbs on expression and artistic freedom. The report documented a sharp rise in reported violations, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total, with detention decisions recorded through formal channels and others taken off the record.

Aydın's Human Rights Association branch was among the bodies that coordinated demands for an independent investigation into the death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025, a reminder that local activist networks in the province are connected to national accountability work. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Trans people resident in Aydın live under the same registration rules as elsewhere in Turkey: gender is fixed by registered sex, and a trans man held in a women's prison was documented in the parliamentary record of the Poyraz case in December 2025. Transition-related care is tightening through the Ministry of Health's September 2025 reporting rules, which require official e-reports to record the patient's gender rather than accepting an "other" entry — a change adopted after a provincial health directorate in Kayseri added "gender reassignment" to the official reasons for medical-board reporting.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees, including any resident of Aydın convicted of an offence, are governed by segregation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider profile on Turkey, built with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data, records arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, refusals of hospital transfer, no staff training in LGBT prisoner needs, and complaints procedures that are ineffective and may provoke further violence.

Public assembly remains constrained. Rights monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law recorded since 2015 had continued through 2025, accompanied by discriminatory rhetoric from senior officials. Kaos GL's monitoring found regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting expression and artistic freedom during the same year.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no Aydın-specific incidents of violence, police stops, or local administrative action against trans people; the province appears in the record only as the site of a Human Rights Association branch that joined the national demand for an independent investigation into the death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025. Whether any equivalent local initiative has been registered in Aydın during 2025 is unresolved on the present sources.

The status of the draft legislative package described by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 remains unresolved in this inventory: it was pending at the date of the release, with no source here recording whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn. Its reported provisions — criminalising same-sex ceremonies with penalties up to four years, raising the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility, and penalising the clinicians who provide that care — should be treated as draft provisions in force at time of reporting rather than as established law.

Current provincial enforcement practice in Aydın for gendered ID checks of foreign visitors is not sourced here. The requirement to carry original photo identification, with fines up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention, is documented for Turkey nationally and applies in holiday destinations; the frequency and character of checkpoint activity specifically in Aydın's coastal towns is not established.
